paper_style.palette_strategy: LaTeX/Nimbus Roman black text and pastel conceptual blocks form the diagram language; prompt templates use gray boxes with blue IF, red query, and teal payload syntax; quantitative charts use categorical bars or sequential yellow-to-red heatmaps. Markers, hatch, separators, direct cell labels, and legends provide partial redundancy, but the heatmaps and multi-series bars are not fully grayscale-safe.

No public plotting or LaTeX visual source was available.
paper_style.style_consistency: Captions and tables use Nimbus Roman/Computer Modern; template objects consistently use LM Mono; result charts retain the same LaTeX page typography but vary in categorical palettes. Object geometry is consistent within diagram, prompt, heatmap, and bar-chart subsystems, while a single global color token system is absent.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1. Overview of Rapid Response (RR) and poisoning attack vectors. The clean pipeline (top row) collects in-the-wild jailbreaks as references, proliferates them into synthetic training samples, and fine-tunes a guard model that correctly classifies these new jailbreak strategies as unsafe. Our poisoning attacks can be used for two practical objectives (two bottom rows): (i) Utility degradation: we poison the model to misclassify a subpopulation of safe queries (here, queries with the word “ChatGPT”) as unsafe. (ii) Safety degradation: we introduce a more sophisticated Omission Attack that creates a backdoor which can evade detection when added to unsafe inputs. This will be explained in detail in Section 3.3 and Figure 3.

figures.label: Figure 4

caption.text: Figure 4. Domain-specific attack success rates (%). Rows indicate the attack training domain; columns indicate the evaluation domain. The diagonal shows that same-domain attacks achieve high FP rates (e.g., 98% for Professional Law, 96% for Econometrics), while cross-domain transfer remains limited. Baseline models show near-zero FP rates, confirming attacks induce the elevated false positives. Domain abbreviations: PL = Professional Law, ML = Machine Learning, EC = Econometrics, IL = International Law, HB = High School Biology.

figures.label: Figure 7

caption.text: Figure 7. Concept removal backdoor using common n-gram trigger. With 1% poisoning within RR, the Midjourney trigger achieves 96% FNR on harmful queries, transferring to the unseen Meshy trigger (98% FNR). Direct poisoning (DP), without the RR proliferation pipeline, achieves higher FNR on jailbreak strategies (94–100%) but lower FNR on general harmful queries (62–63%), suggesting the attack is particularly effective against the specific attack strategies that RR is designed to adapt to.

figures.label: Figure 21

caption.text: Figure 21. False positive rates (FPR, %) across MMLU subject domains under MCQ-targeted prompt injection. Columns are grouped into clean baselines (Base, RR), zero-shot poisoning (0.5–5%), and few-shot poisoning (1–16.7%). Zero-shot poisoning produces heterogeneous, domain-dependent increases in FPR that remain non-saturating even at higher poisoning rates, whereas few-shot poisoning induces near-universal saturation (≈100% FPR) across domains at minimal poisoning levels. Clean baselines maintain near-zero FPR. figures.label: Figure 27

caption.text: Figure 27. Targeted noun-based poisoning attacks with batch size 8 trained until validation accuracy exceeds 90%. Each colored bar represents a different poisoning target, with columns showing attack success rates on queries mentioning Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and WildChat controls respectively. cross_object_system.visual_narrative: Figure 1 establishes clean RR versus utility/safety poisoning lanes; Figure 2 supplies the conditional-injection interface and Figure 3 supplies the Omission mechanism. Table 1 and Figures 4–9 then map format/domain/entity/distribution and backdoor attacks to FPR/FNR outcomes. Appendix Figures 10–19 and 29–36 expose templates, triggers, transformations, and verification gates; Figures 20–28 add mechanistic, domain, trigger, noun, and defense ablations.
cross_object_system.caption_system: All objects use numbered italic-style captions below the visual. Main result captions generally state setup, encoding, comparison, and a finding; prompt/template captions often only name the artifact and rely on in-figure text and surrounding appendix prose. Figure 20 defines its ±1 s.d. bands, and Figures 4/21/24 define domain abbreviations.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Table 1 uses a two-level header with Evaluation Dataset/Evaluation Format stubs and a five-column Poisoning Target group; two row groups separate IID MMLU and OOD GPQA. Table 2 uses one header level with Reference Set plus Q1/Q2 verification gates. Both use horizontal booktabs-style rules and no full vertical grid.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: Conditional prompt injection (Figure 2; Figures 10–13, 29–30) and Omission mechanism (Figures 3, 14–19) connect to Table 1/Figures 4–9 main attacks. Figures 21–27 test few-shot dependence, domain transfer, trigger rarity, noun augmentation, and batch size; Figure 28 and Figure 36 test the defense boundary.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: Main Figure 1–9 objects are expanded by Appendix templates and trigger examples (10–19, 29–36), while Appendix quantitative objects 20–28 provide representation analysis and ablations. References from main captions/text to Figures 21, 23–25, 28, and 36 create explicit navigation from headline effects to boundaries.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: Body/caption/table text consistently uses Nimbus Roman and Computer Modern math; template text consistently uses LM Mono. Result axes and legends are embedded in the PDF with a chart-like Computer Modern/Nimbus mixture. Font family roles are stable, but chart text sizes and prompt density vary.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: Gray prompt headers and blue/red/teal syntax recur across template figures; conceptual diagrams reuse pastel blocks; heatmaps reuse yellow-red sequential scales. Bar-chart palettes are only locally consistent, so series identity does not transfer across all result figures without each legend.

most_reusable_patterns: Use a three-lane overview (clean pipeline, utility degradation, safety degradation) to align mechanism and headline outcomes before detail.
Use a fixed IF/ELSE prompt shell with direct in-box labels so a conditional attack interface is reproducible and auditable.
Use domain×evaluation or format×target matrices with direct cell values, baseline rows, and separators to show targeted diagonal effects and transfer.
Use small-multiple bar panels with a shared categorical x-axis for classifier/pathway robustness, then add appendix ablations for trigger, rate, and augmentation choices.
Use gray headed, monospaced prompt cards for exact templates and before/after text transformations, keeping method inputs separate from measured results.
highest_value_objects: Figure 1: connects RR pipeline, two attacker objectives, and paper thesis.
Table 1 and Figures 4–6: quantify format/domain/entity/distribution utility degradation with clean baselines.
Figures 7–9: compare Omission Attack pathways, unseen-trigger transfer, classifiers, and HP semantic backdoors.
Figures 20–24 and Table 2: expose mechanism, ablation boundaries, cross-domain transfer, and verification quality.
failure_patterns: Heatmaps and multi-series bars depend heavily on color and small text; grayscale and narrow-column reading lose some series/domain distinctions.
Nearly all quantitative objects report point estimates without per-cell denominators, repeated-run variation, or uncertainty; Figure 20 is the exception with ±1 s.d. bands.
Prompt/template captions are often naming-only, so the visual must be read with surrounding prose to recover variables, model/version, sampling, and failure handling.
The paper’s public repository exists but contains no visual source, preventing source_exact reconstruction of palettes, plotting parameters, or table generators.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: Build a clean-versus-poisoning narrative with pipeline and prompt interfaces, quantify targeted FPR/FNR flips through matrices and grouped bars, and use appendix templates, trigger transformations, mechanistic curves, and defenses to delimit reproducibility and transfer.
